title: About this portfolio
text:
This website is my learning portfolio for ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications. It records the methods, code, visualisations, and interpretations developed through the course’s hands-on exercises.
The portfolio is created with R and Quarto, version-controlled on GitHub, and published as a website through Vercel.

title: About this portfolio
text:
Course themes

Geospatial data import, transformation, and geoprocessing
Thematic mapping and geovisualisation
First- and second-order spatial point-pattern analysis
Spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis

The worked pages are organised under the Hands-on Exercises dropdown in the navigation bar.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 1: Geospatial Data Science with R. It demonstrates how to import, inspect, project, convert, and geoprocess spatial data in R. The analysis answers two practical questions:

How much land lies within five metres of Singapore’s cycling-path network?
How are pre-schools distributed across Master Plan 2014 subzones?

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Data and packages
The current data.gov.sg downloads are GeoJSON rather than the shapefile and KML formats used in the original course notes. GeoJSON is used here because it is the current official downloadable format and preserves the geometry in one file.
The requested Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) collection currently has no downloadable child dataset. I therefore use Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea). This substitution is appropriate for area-based pre-school density because offshore polygons would enlarge coastal subzones without adding pre-schools.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Importing geospatial data
st_read() reads all three vector datasets as simple-feature data frames. The course’s chap01/data/... path belongs to the lecturer’s project; the paths below match this repository.


Show the R code
mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

cyclingpath <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "CyclingPathNetwork.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

preschool <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "PreSchoolsLocation.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)



Inspecting the feature data frames
Before analysing the data, I check the number of features, geometry type, attributes, and coordinate reference system (CRS).


Show the R code
spatial_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  Features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(cyclingpath), nrow(preschool)),
  Attributes = c(ncol(mpsz) - 1, ncol(cyclingpath) - 1, ncol(preschool) - 1),
  Geometry = c(
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(cyclingpath))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(preschool))), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  `Native CRS` = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(cyclingpath)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input),
  check.names = FALSE
)

Working with projection
Distance and area should not be calculated in longitude and latitude. I transform all three objects to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414), a projected CRS measured in metres.


Show the R code
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

crs_check <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  EPSG = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(cyclingpath)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg),
  Units = c("metres", "metres", "metres")
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Importing and converting aspatial data
The Airbnb CSV contains longitude and latitude fields but no geometry column, so it begins as an ordinary data frame.


Show the R code
listings <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "listings.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(
  listings,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

listing_summary <- data.frame(
  Records = nrow(listings_sf),
  Geometry = paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(listings_sf))), collapse = ", "),
  EPSG = st_crs(listings_sf)$epsg,
  `Longitude/latitude retained` = all(c("longitude", "latitude") %in% names(listings_sf)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Geoprocessing

Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?
A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with st_union() to obtain the unique footprint.


Show the R code
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

naive_buffer_ha <- st_area(buffer_cycling) |>
  sum() |>
  set_units("ha")

dissolved_buffer_ha <- buffer_cycling |>
  st_union() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units("ha")

overlap_pct <- as.numeric(
  (naive_buffer_ha - dissolved_buffer_ha) / naive_buffer_ha * 100
)

buffer_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Sum of individual buffers", "Dissolved unique footprint"),
  `Area (hectares)` = round(c(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha)), 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(buffer_results, caption = "Area within five metres of cycling paths")



Area within five metres of cycling paths


Method
Area (hectares)




Sum of individual buffers
498.97


Dissolved unique footprint
431.51





Answer. The non-overlapping five-metre buffer covers approximately 431.51 hectares. A simple sum gives 498.97 hectares because overlapping buffers are counted more than once, overstating the unique footprint by about 13.5%.


Question 2: How many pre-schools are in each subzone?
st_intersects() returns the pre-school row indices that fall inside each subzone. lengths() converts that list into one count per subzone.


Show the R code
mpsz$PreSch_Count <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

top_count <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_Count) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Count)) |>
  head(10)

kable(
  top_count,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Pre-schools"),
  caption = "Subzones with the most pre-schools"
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Key findings

The current official spatial files contain 323 subzones, 8,523 cycling-path features, and 2,290 pre-school locations.
Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about 431.51 hectares.
TAMPINES EAST has the most pre-schools (72), while CECIL has the highest density (35.6 per km²).
Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Limitations
The datasets come from different reference dates, so the analysis is a methodological exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text: This exercise follows Chapter 5: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis. Exercise 4 established that childcare-centre intensity varies across Singapore. Here, G-, F-, K-, and L-functions test whether centres also depart from complete spatial randomness (CSR) across distance scales within Choa Chu Kang and Tampines.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text: This exercise follows Chapter 5: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis. Exercise 4 established that childcare-centre intensity varies across Singapore. Here, G-, F-, K-, and L-functions test whether centres also depart from complete spatial randomness (CSR) across distance scales within Choa Chu Kang and Tampines.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Data and observation windows
The analysis reuses the ECDA Child Care Services points and URA Master Plan 2019 Planning Area Boundary from Exercise 4. All coordinates are transformed to EPSG:3414 so distance is measured in metres.


Show the R code
planning_area <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_PlanningArea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(3414)

childcare <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "ChildCareServices.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

make_local_ppp <- function(area_name) {
  boundary <- planning_area |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == area_name)
  local_points <- childcare[lengths(st_within(childcare, boundary)) > 0, ]
  xy <- st_coordinates(local_points)
  ppp(
    x = xy[, 1],
    y = xy[, 2],
    window = as.owin(st_union(boundary)),
    checkdup = FALSE
  )
}

patterns <- list(
  "Choa Chu Kang" = make_local_ppp("CHOA CHU KANG"),
  "Tampines" = make_local_ppp("TAMPINES")
)

window_summary <- data.frame(
  `Planning area` = names(patterns),
  Centres = sapply(patterns, npoints),
  `Window area (km²)` = round(sapply(patterns, function(x) area.owin(Window(x))) / 1e6, 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
What the four functions test

G-function: nearest-neighbour distances from events; an observed curve above CSR suggests unusually short event-to-event distances.
F-function: distances from empty locations to the nearest event; an observed curve below CSR suggests larger gaps between clusters.
K-function: cumulative event interaction over distance; values above CSR suggest clustering.
L-function: a variance-stabilised transformation of K; values above CSR again suggest clustering.

For each statistic, 99 CSR simulations create a pointwise simulation envelope. The seed makes the exercise reproducible. This is a concise exploratory test; a confirmatory analysis should use more simulations and a global envelope.


Show the R code
set.seed(608)
nsim <- 99

make_envelopes <- function(x) {
  list(
    G = envelope(x, Gest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    F = envelope(x, Fest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    K = envelope(x, Kest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    L = envelope(x, Lest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE)
  )
}

envelopes <- lapply(patterns, make_envelopes)

Choa Chu Kang

plot(envelopes[["Choa Chu Kang"]]$G, main = "G: nearest neighbour")
plot(envelopes[["Choa Chu Kang"]]$F, main = "F: empty space")
plot(envelopes[["Choa Chu Kang"]]$K, main = "K: cumulative interaction")

CSR envelopes for Choa Chu Kang; black is observed, grey is the simulated envelope




Show the R code
par(old_par)


The observed G curve rises above the envelope at short distances and F falls below it across part of the range. K is above the envelope for much of the evaluated distance range. Together these are consistent with clusters of nearby centres separated by relatively larger gaps.

Tampines


Show the R code

plot(envelopes[["Tampines"]]$G, main = "G: nearest neighbour")
plot(envelopes[["Tampines"]]$F, main = "F: empty space")
plot(envelopes[["Tampines"]]$K, main = "K: cumulative interaction")
plot(envelopes[["Tampines"]]$L, main = "L: variance-stabilised K")





CSR envelopes for Tampines; black is observed, grey is the simulated envelope




Show the R code
par(old_par)


Tampines shows a stronger and more persistent departure: G is frequently above the upper envelope, F is below its lower envelope over most of the tested range, and both K and L remain above CSR. The result indicates multi-scale clustering rather than a pattern confined to only immediate neighbours.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Compact numerical diagnostic
The table summarises the share of evaluated radii in the clustering direction outside the pointwise CSR envelope. It is a descriptive aid, not a separate p-value.


Show the R code
summarise_envelope <- function(e, direction) {
  valid <- e$r > 0 & is.finite(e$obs) & is.finite(e$lo) & is.finite(e$hi)
  departure <- if (direction == "above") e$obs[valid] > e$hi[valid] else e$obs[valid] < e$lo[valid]
  data.frame(
    `Radii outside envelope (%)` = round(mean(departure) * 100, 1),
    `First departure (m)` = if (any(departure)) round(min(e$r[valid][departure])) else NA_real_,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

diagnostic_rows <- list()
for (area_name in names(envelopes)) {
  for (statistic in c("G", "F", "K", "L")) {
    direction <- if (statistic == "F") "below" else "above"
    diagnostic_rows[[length(diagnostic_rows) + 1]] <- cbind(
      data.frame(`Planning area` = area_name, Function = statistic, Direction = direction, check.names = FALSE),
      summarise_envelope(envelopes[[area_name]][[statistic]], direction)
    )
  }
}

diagnostics <- bind_rows(diagnostic_rows)
kable(diagnostics, caption = "Observed departures in the direction associated with clustering")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Answer and limitations
Both planning areas reject the visual expectation of CSR over meaningful distance ranges, with markedly stronger and more consistent clustering in Tampines. G and F describe the nearest-event and empty-space components, while K and L show that the departure persists across broader distances.
The reference process is deliberately simple. Childcare services respond to population and urban form, so CSR is a baseline rather than a realistic causal model. Results also depend on the planning-area boundary, edge correction, duplicate-location handling, and the number of simulations.

This exercise follows Chapter 4: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis and studies the distribution of childcare services in Singapore. It answers two questions:

Are childcare centres consistent with complete spatial randomness (CSR)?

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test
The null hypothesis is CSR. Values of the Clark–Evans ratio (R<1) indicate shorter nearest-neighbour distances than expected under CSR; (R>1) indicates a more regular pattern. The CDF edge correction is suitable for the non-rectangular Singapore window.


Show the R code
ce_sg <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_ppp,
  correction = "cdf",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_result <- data.frame(
  Area = "Singapore",
  `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3),
  `p-value` = format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Decision = ifelse(ce_sg$p.value < 0.05, "Reject CSR", "Do not reject CSR"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(ce_result, caption = "Clark–Evans test with CDF edge correction")

Answer. (R=) 0.486 with < 0.001, so the childcare pattern is significantly clustered relative to CSR. This is not evidence that centres attract one another; population, housing estates, zoning, and service demand are plausible spatially varying drivers.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Kernel density estimation
bw.diggle() selects a data-driven fixed bandwidth. An adaptive KDE is also estimated: it uses narrower kernels where points are dense and wider kernels in sparse areas. Both surfaces are expressed as estimated centres per square kilometre.


Show the R code
fixed_bandwidth <- bw.diggle(childcare_ppp)

fixed_kde <- density(
  childcare_ppp,
  sigma = fixed_bandwidth,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

adaptive_kde <- adaptive.density(
  childcare_ppp,
  f = 0.15,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

fixed_grid <- as.data.frame(fixed_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = paste0("Fixed KDE (h = ", round(fixed_bandwidth), " m)"))

adaptive_grid <- as.data.frame(adaptive_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = "Adaptive KDE")

kde_grid <- bind_rows(fixed_grid, adaptive_grid)




Show the R code
ggplot(kde_grid, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(planning_area), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", na.value = NA) +
  labs(
    fill = "Estimated centres\nper km²",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Fixed and adaptive estimates of childcare-centre intensity




Answer. The fixed-bandwidth surface peaks in Sengkang. The fixed surface is easier to compare across the island; the adaptive surface retains sharper local peaks in dense estates and smooths more aggressively in sparse peripheral areas. KDE measures concentration of facilities, not accessibility or demand satisfaction.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Planning-area comparison
The course guide compares Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang, and Jurong West. Counts and area-standardised densities show why raw totals alone can mislead.


Show the R code
focus_names <- c("PUNGGOL", "TAMPINES", "CHOA CHU KANG", "JURONG WEST")

childcare_with_area <- st_join(
  childcare,
  planning_area["PLN_AREA_N"],
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)

focus_summary <- planning_area |>
  filter(PLN_AREA_N %in% focus_names) |>
  mutate(Area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(PLN_AREA_N, Area_km2) |>
  left_join(
    childcare_with_area |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      count(PLN_AREA_N, name = "Centres"),
    by = "PLN_AREA_N"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Centres per km²` = Centres / Area_km2,
    Area_km2 = round(Area_km2, 2),
    `Centres per km²` = round(`Centres per km²`, 2)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Centres per km²`))

kable(
  focus_summary,
  col.names = c("Planning area", "Area (km²)", "Centres", "Centres per km²"),
  caption = "Childcare provision in the four focus planning areas"
)

make_local_ppp <- function(area_name) {
  boundary <- planning_area |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == area_name)
  local_points <- childcare[lengths(st_within(childcare, boundary)) > 0, ]
  local_xy <- st_coordinates(local_points)
  ppp(
    local_xy[, 1], local_xy[, 2],
    window = as.owin(st_union(boundary)),
    checkdup = FALSE
  )
}

local_tests <- lapply(c("CHOA CHU KANG", "TAMPINES"), function(area_name) {
  local_ppp <- make_local_ppp(area_name)
  test <- clarkevans.test(local_ppp, correction = "cdf", alternative = "clustered")
  data.frame(
    `Planning area` = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(area_name)),
    Centres = npoints(local_ppp),
    `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
    `p-value` = format.pval(test$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Conclusion
The nearest-neighbour and KDE results agree: childcare services are not distributed uniformly. The strongest fixed-KDE concentration is in Sengkang, and substantial local clustering remains in Choa Chu Kang and Tampines. These are descriptive first-order findings; a demand-adjusted study would add child population, capacity, transport access, and housing density.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R. It joins population attributes to Singapore’s Master Plan 2019 subzones and asks:

Where are dependency ratios relatively high?
How much does the classification method change the visual message?
Which subzones deserve closer inspection?

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R. It joins population attributes to Singapore’s Master Plan 2019 subzones and asks:

Where are dependency ratios relatively high?
How much does the classification method change the visual message?
Which subzones deserve closer inspection?

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Data and preparation
The map uses the current official downloadable boundaries and the 2020 Census population table. The course notes use a later SingStat file, but the public table below contains the same subzone-by-age structure needed to reproduce the method.



Dataset
Source
Use




Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)
URA via data.gov.sg
Mapping units


Resident Population by Planning Area/Subzone, Age and Sex, Census 2020
Singapore Department of Statistics via data.gov.sg
Age-group counts





Show the R code
mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_Subzone.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid()

population <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "resident_population_2020.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = "-"
)

numeric_fields <- setdiff(names(population), "Number")
population[numeric_fields] <- lapply(population[numeric_fields], as.numeric)

# Remove national and planning-area totals, leaving one row per subzone.
population <- population |>
  filter(Number != "Total", !grepl(" - Total$", Number)) |>
  mutate(join_key = toupper(trimws(Number)))

young_fields <- c(
  "Total_0_4", "Total_5_9", "Total_10_14", "Total_15_19", "Total_20_24"
)
active_fields <- c(
  "Total_25_29", "Total_30_34", "Total_35_39", "Total_40_44",
  "Total_45_49", "Total_50_54", "Total_55_59", "Total_60_64"
)
aged_fields <- c(
  "Total_65_69", "Total_70_74", "Total_75_79",
  "Total_80_84", "Total_85_89", "Total_90andOver"
)

population <- population |>
  mutate(
    YOUNG = rowSums(across(all_of(young_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    ECONOMY_ACTIVE = rowSums(across(all_of(active_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    AGED = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    DEPENDENCY = 100 * (YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY_ACTIVE
  )

residential <- mpsz |>
  left_join(population, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "join_key")) |>
  filter(Total_Total > 0, is.finite(DEPENDENCY))


The dependency ratio is the number of residents aged 0–24 or 65+ per 100 residents aged 25–64. 234 populated subzones have a valid ratio; unpopulated and unmatched planning polygons are excluded from the thematic analysis.


Show the R code
quality <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Boundary features", "Subzones joined to population", "Populated subzones analysed"),
  Result = c(
    nrow(mpsz),
    sum(!is.na(left_join(mpsz, population, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "join_key"))$Total_Total)),
    nrow(residential)
  )
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Choropleth map
A sequential palette is appropriate because dependency ratio has a natural low-to-high order. Quantile classes put a similar number of subzones in each colour, making relative rank easy to see.


Show the R code
quantile_breaks <- classIntervals(
  residential$DEPENDENCY,
  n = 5,
  style = "quantile"
)$brks

residential <- residential |>
  mutate(
    Dependency_class = cut(
      DEPENDENCY,
      breaks = unique(quantile_breaks),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      dig.lab = 4
    )
  )

ggplot(residential) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Dependency_class), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1, drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Dependency ratios vary sharply across residential Singapore",
    subtitle = "Dependents aged 0–24 or 65+ per 100 residents aged 25–64",
    fill = "Ratio (quantiles)",
    caption = "Source: Singapore Census of Population 2020 and URA MP2019"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Dependency ratio by populated subzone, Census 2020




Answer. Across populated subzones, the median dependency ratio is 70.3 dependents per 100 working-age residents. Very small resident populations can produce unstable ratios, so the ranking below requires at least 5,000 residents.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Classification matters
Equal-interval and quantile classifications answer different visual questions. Equal intervals preserve the numeric scale; quantiles emphasise relative position among subzones.


Show the R code
equal_breaks <- classIntervals(
  residential$DEPENDENCY,
  n = 5,
  style = "equal"
)$brks

quantile_map <- residential |>
  mutate(
    Class_number = as.integer(cut(DEPENDENCY, unique(quantile_breaks), include.lowest = TRUE)),
    Method = "Quantile: similar number of subzones per class"
  )

equal_map <- residential |>
  mutate(
    Class_number = as.integer(cut(DEPENDENCY, unique(equal_breaks), include.lowest = TRUE)),
    Method = "Equal interval: same numeric width per class"
  )

comparison_map <- rbind(quantile_map, equal_map)

ggplot(comparison_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(Class_number)), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  scale_fill_brewer(
    palette = "YlOrRd",
    drop = FALSE,
    labels = c("1 (lowest)", "2", "3", "4", "5 (highest)")
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(fill = "Within-method class") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.1, "cm")
  )





The same dependency ratios classified in two ways




The equal-interval map is dominated by the low-population outlier Loyang West. Quantiles provide a more useful comparison among the ordinary residential subzones, while the exact values remain available in the table and interactive map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Conclusion
The exercise shows why a thematic map is an analytical argument rather than decoration. Quantiles reveal relative differences cleanly, equal intervals expose the influence of extreme values, selection prevents tiny denominators from dominating the ranking, and the interactive version preserves exact values for exploration.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 6: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis and studies 2023 satellite fire detections in Indonesia’s Kepulauan Bangka Belitung province. It answers the guide’s two research questions:

Are the spatial locations and detection dates independent?
Where and when do fire detections cluster?

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 6: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis and studies 2023 satellite fire detections in Indonesia’s Kepulauan Bangka Belitung province. It answers the guide’s two research questions:

Are the spatial locations and detection dates independent?
Where and when do fire detections cluster?

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Data and study area
The lecturer’s project-local files are not published through the chapter URL, so this reproducible version uses a public snapshot of the same NASA FIRMS 2023 Indonesia feed and filters it spatially to Bangka Belitung. GADM level-1 and level-2 boundaries replace the course’s union of subdistrict polygons; the province footprint has the same analytical role, while districts make the results easier to name.



Dataset
Source
Use




Indonesia active-fire detections, 2023
NASA FIRMS via the course-project public snapshot
Space-time events


Indonesia administrative boundaries, GADM 4.1
GADM
Province window and district labels





Show the R code
province <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "temporal", "BangkaBelitung.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(32748)

districts <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "temporal", "BangkaBelitung_Districts.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(32748)

fires <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "temporal", "forestfires_2023.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    acq_date = as.Date(acq_date),
    Month_num = as.integer(format(acq_date, "%m")),
    Month = factor(month.abb[Month_num], levels = month.abb),
    DayOfYear = as.integer(format(acq_date, "%j"))
  )

fire_sf <- st_as_sf(
  fires,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(32748)

district_labels <- c(
  Bangka = "Bangka",
  BangkaBarat = "Bangka Barat",
  BangkaSelatan = "Bangka Selatan",
  BangkaTengah = "Bangka Tengah",
  Belitung = "Belitung",
  BelitungTimur = "Belitung Timur",
  Pangkalpinang = "Pangkalpinang"
)

districts <- districts |>
  mutate(District = recode(NAME_2, !!!district_labels))

fire_sf <- st_join(
  fire_sf,
  districts["District"],
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

quality <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Fire detections", "Date range", "Detections assigned to a district", "Projected CRS"),
  Value = c(
    nrow(fire_sf),
    paste(min(fires$acq_date), "to", max(fires$acq_date)),
    sum(!is.na(fire_sf$District)),
    st_crs(fire_sf)$epsg
  )
)

When did detections occur?

Show the R code
temporal_kde <- density(

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Spatio-temporal kernel density
The chapter uses spattemp.density(). The calculation below implements the same product-kernel idea directly: every monthly slice combines a 12 km Gaussian spatial kernel with a one-month Gaussian temporal kernel. Values are rescaled to 0–1 across all six slices to emphasise changes in the location and strength of concentrations.


Show the R code
province_window <- as.owin(st_union(province))
fire_xy <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

fire_ppp <- ppp(
  x = fire_xy[, 1],
  y = fire_xy[, 2],
  window = province_window,
  checkdup = FALSE
)

target_months <- 7:12
spatial_bandwidth <- 12000
temporal_bandwidth <- 1

monthly_surfaces <- lapply(target_months, function(target_month) {
  temporal_weight <- dnorm(
    (fires$Month_num - target_month) / temporal_bandwidth
  )

  surface <- density(
    fire_ppp,
    sigma = spatial_bandwidth,
    weights = temporal_weight,
    edge = TRUE,
    dimyx = 110
  )

  as.data.frame(surface) |>
    mutate(Month = factor(month.abb[target_month], levels = month.abb[target_months]))
}) |>
  bind_rows()

monthly_surfaces <- monthly_surfaces |>
  mutate(Relative_intensity = value / max(value, na.rm = TRUE))




Show the R code
ggplot(monthly_surfaces, aes(x, y, fill = Relative_intensity)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Month, ncol = 3) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(province), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA) +
  labs(fill = "Relative\nintensity", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Product-kernel space-time intensity slices, July–December 2023




The surfaces show activity building on Bangka Island from July, strengthening across western and southern Bangka in August–September, and reaching its strongest and broadest concentration in Bangka Selatan in October. Intensity falls in November and contracts sharply by December.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Are space and time independent?
Under space-time independence, randomly reassigning dates to the observed locations should leave the number of near-space/near-time pairs broadly unchanged. I use a transparent permutation test:

a spatial pair is “near” when locations are within 10 km;
a temporal pair is “near” when detections are within seven days;
dates are permuted among fixed locations 199 times.

This tests the same independence question as a space-time K-function while keeping the result concise and directly interpretable.


Show the R code
spatial_distance <- as.matrix(dist(fire_xy))
date_number <- as.integer(fires$acq_date)
upper_pairs <- upper.tri(spatial_distance)
near_in_space <- upper_pairs & spatial_distance <= 10000

count_close_pairs <- function(dates) {
  temporal_distance <- abs(outer(dates, dates, "-"))
  sum(near_in_space & temporal_distance <= 7)
}

observed_pairs <- count_close_pairs(date_number)

set.seed(608)
permuted_pairs <- replicate(
  199,
  count_close_pairs(sample(date_number))
)

permutation_p <- (1 + sum(permuted_pairs >= observed_pairs)) / (length(permuted_pairs) + 1)
pair_ratio <- observed_pairs / mean(permuted_pairs)

test_result <- data.frame(
  `Observed close pairs` = observed_pairs,
  `Mean under permutation` = round(mean(permuted_pairs), 1),
  `Observed / expected` = round(pair_ratio, 2),
  `Monte Carlo p-value` = permutation_p,
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(test_result, caption = "Space-time permutation test: 10 km and 7 days")

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Answers and limitations
1. Are location and time independent? No. The observed data contain 1831 close space-time pairs, 1.87 times the permutation expectation, with (p=) 0.005. Dates and locations therefore show significant interaction at the chosen 10 km / 7-day scale.
2. Where and when is clustering strongest? The largest annual and monthly concentration occurs in Bangka Selatan, peaking in October. The temporal KDE peaks around 11 October, and the space-time density surfaces show the hotspot expanding from July through October before receding.
NASA FIRMS records satellite detections, not verified fire incidents or burned area. Cloud cover, satellite revisit timing, duplicate detections of one fire, confidence, and the chosen bandwidths all affect the pattern. The analysis identifies space-time concentration; it does not establish ignition causes.
